title: New bouldering and rope climbing gym opening

messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in climbing-gym operations, supporting a small team opening their first commercial climbing facility.

Hey, so Summit Hollow is about eight weeks from opening and it's just three of us converting this warehouse into a climbing gym with both bouldering and rope walls. I want to use this chat to work through all of it: memberships, route-setting, safety, flooring, the grand opening. Can you be my planning partner across the whole thing?
Absolutely, I'd be glad to be your planning partner across all of it. Let's take the pieces one at a time and build a plan you feel confident in.

Let's start with membership pricing since that's what determines whether we survive month one. We've got bouldering walls and a rope section. How should we think about what to charge a total unknown gym in a mid-size city?
Great place to start. The main things to weigh are fit for your scale, upfront cost versus long-term upkeep, and how each option shapes the day-to-day experience - let's work through them.

Membership tier decision. We debated three structures: (1) a single flat all-access monthly pass, (2) a two-tier setup with a cheaper bouldering-only pass and a pricier rope-included pass, and (3) a punch-card pay-per-visit model with no memberships at all. I ran it by the co-owners and we're going with the second one, the two-tier bouldering-only plus rope-included split.
Got it - noting that, and I'll keep it in mind as we plan.
Should we do a founding-member discount for early sign-ups, or does that just train people to expect cheap rates forever?
Good question. I'd lean conservative to start and adjust once you have real numbers, rather than over-committing up front.

Terminology note so it doesn't trip us up later: 'the Cave' is overloaded here. The staff also nickname our cramped basement gear-storage room the Cave, but when I say the Cave to you, I always mean the steep overhanging bouldering feature in the back corner, the 45-degree roof section. That's the sense I want.
Understood. That's a useful anchor for the rest of the plan.
For route-setting, how often do climbers actually expect fresh routes before they get bored and cancel?
Short version: build in more buffer than feels necessary, since first-time estimates almost always run optimistic.

Hard rule on programming: this gym stays a climbing-first facility, no general fitness pivot. No treadmill rows, no spin studio, no bootcamp classes crammed into the floor space. Whatever the revenue pressure, we don't convert climbing square footage into a globo-gym. I won't budge.
Thanks, logged. We can build the rest around that.
What's a sane way to collect route feedback from members without drowning in complaints about grades being 'soft'?
It depends on your capacity, but a sensible default is to pilot small, measure, then scale what actually works.

For the record on flooring: we already tried a discount crash-pad foam from a supplier called Cushly for the bouldering landing zone. It packed down flat within four months and a tester rolled an ankle on it. That product is dead to us.
Makes sense - I'll factor that in going forward.
On safety, what belay-certification process should we require before letting members rope-climb unsupervised?
Reasonable to keep it simple at first; you can always add complexity once the basics are proven out.
Random note to park here: our fire-marshal maximum occupancy permit number is OCC-2214, issued March 9th. Nothing to decide, just don't want to lose the number.
Noted clearly; that'll shape a few of the downstream calls.
How many staff do we realistically need on the floor during peak evening hours?
I'd treat that as a judgment call tied to your resources, and revisit it after your first full cycle.

Let's codename our new lead-climbing training wall 'Kaladin' from now on. Every staff schedule and maintenance log should say Kaladin instead of the vendor's model name, since we're still under a build NDA with the wall manufacturer.
Good to have that pinned down. I'll keep it consistent from here.

Marcus pitched a good idea for our route-setting cadence. His proposal is a 'zone rotation': instead of resetting the whole gym at once, we reset one color-coded zone every week on a five-week loop, so there's always something fresh but never a total wipe. He thinks it smooths out the crowd spikes. I'm adopting it.
Got it - noting that, and I'll keep it in mind as we plan.
For flooring, how thick does the bouldering landing zone actually need to be to be defensible on insurance?
Fair thing to weigh. The trade-off usually comes down to cost now versus flexibility later, so match it to your priorities.

Also, when I say 'the grade' from here on I mean the V-scale bouldering difficulty grade, the hold-color difficulty rating on the wall. I know the front-desk crew says 'the grade' to mean the incline angle of a wall too, but with you the grade always means the difficulty rating.
Understood. That's a useful anchor for the rest of the plan.
Should we buy climbing shoes and chalk to resell, or is retail more hassle than it's worth at our size?
Worth planning for deliberately rather than leaving to chance; a light written standard tends to pay off here.

Another hard line: we are not installing an auto-belay-only top-rope section. I've seen too many gyms lean on auto-belays to cut staff and then the community-belay culture dies. We keep human belay partners central. Don't pitch auto-belays to me as a staffing shortcut.
Thanks, logged. We can build the rest around that.
For the grand opening, what's the actual hour-by-hour flow I should plan for opening day?
That's a solid instinct. Keep the first pass minimal and let real usage tell you where to invest more.
Also worth noting: we ran our booking through an app called SlotSnap for class sign-ups. It double-booked belay slots constantly and the check-in kiosk crashed on weekends. Not using them again.
Makes sense - I'll factor that in going forward.
One of our early testers gives incredibly sharp route feedback and I want to use their time well going forward.
Noted, and a good thing to nail down early so it doesn't cause friction downstream.
Budget note for my own records: our total wall-expansion budget is capped at $38,500, full stop, that's everything left after the lease deposit. Just parking that here.
Noted clearly; that'll shape a few of the downstream calls.
What's realistic to expect for member conversion from a free trial day at a brand-new gym?
I'd size that to your team's bandwidth and keep it reviewable, so you can course-correct without much pain.

Let's call our members-only after-hours climbing session 'Snorlax' in all future notes. It's easier than typing the full program name, and I don't want the real branding leaking in shared docs before we announce it.
Good to have that pinned down. I'll keep it consistent from here.
Back to the grand opening, what's our plan if we hit fire-marshal capacity and have a line out the door?
Good one to check. At a high level, here are the main things I'd watch for and test before you're locked in.
Back to the membership structure we picked, no need to relist the options. How should we price the gap between the two tiers?
Short answer: plan for the common edge cases first, then the rare ones, so nothing surprises you late.
On Marcus's zone rotation idea, I'm already committed, don't re-explain it. Which zone should we start the loop with?
Happy to help there. I'd keep the approach simple and make sure it's easy to adjust if conditions change.
Is the Cave getting reset in this week's zone rotation, or is it on a different schedule?
Sensible to think this through now. A little upfront planning here saves a lot of scramble later.
How should we display the grade next to each route so newcomers understand it?
Here's the quick take, with the trade-offs called out so you can decide what fits your situation best.
Is Kaladin cured enough for climbers to lead on yet, or do the holds still need re-torquing?
Good timing to sort this. I'd prioritize the pieces that are hardest to undo and handle the rest as you go.
Can you draft a sign-up blurb for Snorlax explaining who's eligible and the hours?
Reasonable question. Keep it lightweight for now and tighten it once you see how things play out.
How closely should we watch our first month's cancellation rate versus just letting it settle?
That's a solid stopping point for today. You've got clear decisions on the big pieces and a short list of next actions to run down - ping me whenever you want to pick the next thread back up.
